The [Bridges conference series](https://www.bridgesmathart.org/) is one of those things I'd like to have got around to when I was still being paid to be an academic. The work presented there lies at the intersection of art and mathematics. I've had reason to read papers on the [conference archive](https://archive.bridgesmathart.org/#gsc.tab=0) and if you have even a passing interest in this sort of thing I recommend you do the same.

Anyway, on a recent poke around the archive I came across this paper by [Kerry Mitchell](https://www.kerrymitchell.art/): 

> Mitchell K. 2021. [Iterated averaging of polygon vertices](https://archive.bridgesmathart.org/2021/bridges2021-197.pdf). In _Proceedings of Bridges 2021: Mathematics, Art, Music, Architecture, Culture_, ed. D Swart, F Farris, and E Torrence, 197–204. Phoenix, Arizona: Tessellations Publishing.

As the title makes clear, this paper presents a procedure where consecutive vertices of a polygon are iteratively averaged to produce a series of polygons. Overlaying the resulting polygons makes pretty pictures.

Needless to say, on encountering this I implemented it in Netlogo. You can download that model [here](iterated-averaging-of-polygon-vertices.nlogox) if you're interested, but R is perhaps a more generally useful language, so I thought I'd make some code to make the pictures in R also. And since today is Day 3 of the [30 Day Map Challenge](https://30daymapchallenge.com/2026/) themed 'Polygons' and this process makes lots of (not really) polygons and ~~maps~~ plots them, well... why not?

One important _caveat_ is that these aren't _really_ polygons, because, as we'll see, they're tangled up messes of points connected. The edges intersect, and they generally fail any `st_is_valid()` tests for that reason. We don't really care about this, because what we're interested in is making pretty pictures, but it bears mentioning before anyone gets mad at me for calling these things polygons.

## The code
As usual, some packages:

```{r}
#| label: imports
library(dplyr)
library(sf)
library(pracma) # <1>
library(ggplot2)
library(gganimate) # <2>
library(patchwork)

set.seed(0)
```
1. Useful additional matrix functions.
2. `ggplot` animations.

The core procedures in iteratively averaging the vertices of a polygon are (i) averaging consecutive vertices^[Duh.], and (ii) recentring and rescaling the resulting polygon so that it doesn't collapse to a point (more on that rabbithole in a moment).

### Averaging consecutive corners
Because `sf` is a thin wrapper around matrices, it's more convenient to do the manipulations of vertices based on a two-column matrix of the corners of a polygon, than on an `sf` polygon.

```{r}
#| label: average-corners
average_corners <- function(m, x = 0.5) {
  m |>
    rbind(m[1, ]) |> # <1>
    apply(2, conv, c(x, 1 - x)) |> # <2>
    head(-1) |>
    tail(-1) # <3>
}
```
1. Append a copy of the first row of the matrix to the end of the matrix.
2. `pracma::conv` is a convenient way to average consecutive values in each column of the matrix.
3. The `head` and `tail` operations clip the matrix back to its original size so we don't unintentionally add extra corners.

Here's an example of this function in operation:

```{r}
#| label: example-1
m <- 1:10 |> matrix(ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE)
m
m |> average_corners()
``` 

Note in particular how the last row in the result is the average of the last row and first row of the original matrix. The `x` parameter in `average_corners()` allows for making the new corners closer to the first or last corner of each pair, although we won't use that here.

### Rescaling and recentring a polygon
Next, some functions to recentre and rescale the resulting polygons. If we don't do this then polygons will collapse to a point. Iterated averaging of the corners of a polygon is a process, almost but not quite the same as the [_mice problem_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mice_problem) which posits the question of what pattern we get if mice each position at the corner of a regular polygon head towards one another at constant speed. Well... not quite towards one another, but towards where they think the mouse they are pursuing will be by the time they get there. The result is a sequence of copies of the original polygon with the mice following logarithmic spiral curves. Turns out this is a bit a rabbithole. Pursuit problems started out as 'the problem of the three dogs' posed by Lucas in 1877, and has been of interest (inevitably) in military contexts where it relates to problems of how to aim missiles at moving targets. Absolutely the most crazily named 'problem' in this realm is the [_homicidal chauffeur problem_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homicidal_chauffeur_problem), so named (according to wikipedia) as an "unclassified proxy for missile defence" problems!

Anyway, to recentre and rescale polygons (again, handled as a two-column matrix of points) we have the following function.

```{r}
get_centre <- function(m) {
  m |>
    apply(2, range) |> # <1>
    apply(2, mean) # <2>
}

mean_distance_to_centre <- function(m, centre) {
  (m - centre)^2 |> # <3>
    apply(1, sum) |> # <4>
    sqrt() |> # <5>
    mean() # <6>
}

recentre <- function(m, r = 1) { # <7>
  centre <- m |> get_centre()
  d <- mean_distance_to_centre(m, centre)
  (m - centre) * r / d + centre
}
```
1. Get the minimum and maximum coordinate in each column.
2. Take the mean to arrive at a centre location.
3. Squared differences to the centre in x and y.
4. Sum the squares, and...
5. ... take the square root to get the distances.
6. Return the mean distance.
7. This function uses the other two to recentre and rescale the points in a matrix to a constant meant distance to centre specified by the `r` parameter.

### Converting a matrix to a polygon
We eventually want to convert these matrices to polygons, so we need this function:

```{r}
#| label: matrix-as-polygon
matrix_as_polygon <- function(m) {
  rbind(m, m[1, ]) |> # <1>
    list() |>
    st_polygon()
}
```
1. `st_polygon` requires the first vertex to be repeated.

### Making a sequence of polygons
Finally, we can put all these together to get a collection of polygons starting from a random collection of points and iteratively averaging the corners.

```{r}
#| label: get-polygons
get_polygons <- function(n_sides, n_iterations = n_sides * 2, x = 0.5) {
  m <-
    matrix(rnorm(2 * n_sides), ncol = 2) |>
    recentre()
  m_list <- list(m)
  for (i in 1:n_iterations) {
    m_list[[i + 1]] <-
      m_list[[i]] |>
      average_corners(x = x) |>
      recentre()
  }
  m_list |>
    lapply(matrix_as_polygon) |>
    cbind() |>
    st_as_sfc() |>
    data.frame() |>
    st_sf()
}
```

## Results
The first few polygons will be very messy, so it makes sense to drop a few, for our purposes.

```{r}
#| label: generate-gdf
drop_frames <- 50
gdf <- get_polygons(200, 500) |>
  slice(-(1:drop_frames))
```

And finally we can plot one. These are really pretty if we draw the polygon unfilled, using a low opacity colour.

```{r}
#| label: fig-example-picture
#| fig-cap: An example picture based on overlaying steps in the iterative corner averaging process.
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
ggplot(gdf) +
  geom_sf(fill = NA, colour = "#00000010") +
  theme_void()
```

### The process animated
Using `gganimate::animate` we can animate the sequence of polygons to get a better feel for the process.

```{r}
#| label: fig-example-animation
#| fig-cap: Animation of the process.
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
anim <- ggplot(gdf |> mutate(t = row_number())) +
  geom_sf(fill = NA, colour = "black") +
  transition_manual(t) +
  theme_void()

animate(anim, nframes = nrow(gdf), fps = 25)
```

### More pretty pictures
Finally, here are some more examples.
```{r}
#| label: fig-several-examples
#| fig-cap: Eight more examples.
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 7
#| echo: false
plots <- list()
for (i in 1:9) {
  plots[[i]] <-
    ggplot(get_polygons(200, 500) |> slice(-(1:drop_frames))) +
    geom_sf(fill = NA, colour = "#00000010") +
    theme_void()
}
wrap_plots(plots, ncol = 3, nrow = 3)
```
